questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the core limitation of the single-service SRE model (SLIs, SLOs, golden signals for one team) once an organization runs hundreds of services?
options: The golden signals themselves become inaccurate and need to be replaced entirely
SLOs can no longer be measured with any tooling at that scale
A service's reliability stops being mostly a function of its own code, since it now depends on a graph of other services with their own SLOs
On-call rotations are no longer necessary once a company has hundreds of services
questions.explain: At enterprise scale, reliability composes down a dependency graph. A flawless service can still fail users because of a dependency several calls away, so 'my service is fine' stops being a meaningful statement on its own.

questions.q: Why does a shared low-level dependency (such as an auth token issuer or a feature-flag service) create outsized organizational risk at hundreds-of-services scale?
options: It sits underneath many unrelated call paths, so a change to it can take down products owned by teams who have never heard of it
Shared dependencies are always slower than dedicated ones
It means only one team needs to be paged during any incident
Shared services are exempt from having their own SLOs
questions.explain: A shared dependency used by many unrelated teams becomes a single point of organizational blast radius — a seemingly small change can cascade into outages for products the owning team has no visibility into.

questions.q: Why does enterprise SRE practice push toward standardized SLO definitions, alerting severity, and runbook formats across teams rather than letting each team invent its own?
options: Standardization is required by law for any company running more than one service
So an incident commander pulled into a sev-1 can understand any team's dashboard and alerts without relearning bespoke conventions under pressure
It allows every team's SLO to be set to exactly the same numeric target
It removes the need for any team to define SLIs at all
questions.explain: Standardized conventions make reliability legible across the whole organization, which matters most during incident response when someone unfamiliar with a given service needs to act quickly.

questions.q: What is a production readiness review (PRR) as described in this lesson?
options: A performance review conducted for SRE engineers once a year
A load test run automatically by CI on every deploy
A one-time legal sign-off required before a company can sell a product
A checklist-driven review gating whether a new or changed service is trusted with real production traffic, verifying it meets the org's standard reliability practice
questions.explain: A PRR checks exactly the things this lesson covers: documented SLIs/SLOs in the standard format, golden-signal instrumentation, known critical dependencies, runbooks, and a realistic on-call rotation.

questions.q: In this lesson's framing, why is a dependency graph useful to an enterprise SRE organization?
options: It replaces the need for SLOs entirely
It is only useful for billing and cost allocation, not reliability
It lets teams reason about blast radius and which services sit on the critical path for which user-facing outcomes
It is a visualization used exclusively by the marketing team
questions.explain: Mapping which services call which other services is what lets an organization reason concretely about blast radius and critical paths across a graph of hundreds of services, rather than guessing during an incident.
